II-6.explain: Screening only makes sense for diseases that look normal at birth yet cause harm and can be treated early.
II-6.hook: Silent, Serious, Saveable: the 3 S of screening.

checks.q: Which classic criteria define a disease worth screening for?
checks.why: Wilson-Jungner criteria: silent at birth, harmful, treatable. Jones is rheumatic fever, Duke is endocarditis.

II-6.explain: Hungary's expanded programme uses tandem MS to pick up many inborn errors from one blood spot.

checks.q: How many congenital metabolic diseases does Hungary screen routinely?
checks.why: 26 diseases since expanded tandem-MS screening (official answer key).

checks.q: MCAD deficiency belongs to which group of disorders?
checks.why: MCAD is a fatty-acid oxidation defect; PKU is an aminoacidopathy.

II-6.explain: In utero the placenta dialyses toxic metabolites away; once the baby feeds, the enzyme block shows.
II-6.hook: Placenta = free dialysis; milk = the unmasking test.

checks.q: Why are metabolic disorders usually silent at birth?
checks.why: The placenta removes metabolites in utero; feeding then unmasks the defect.

checks.q: Which enzyme is deficient in classic PKU?
checks.why: PKU = phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency; homogentisate oxidase is alkaptonuria.

checks.q: Which sepsis organism is typical in galactosaemia after milk feeds?
checks.why: Galactosaemia classically presents with jaundice, cataract and E. coli sepsis.

II-6.explain: MCAD babies cannot burn fat for ketones when fasting; PKU causes low melanin and a musty smell.
II-6.hook: MCAD: 'Missed meal, no ketones, collapse'. PKU: pale and musty.

checks.q: Fasting in MCAD deficiency causes which glucose/ketone pattern?
checks.why: No fatty-acid oxidation means no ketones: hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, risk of sudden death.

checks.q: Which odour is typical of untreated PKU?
checks.why: PKU smells musty (phenylacetate); maple syrup is MSUD, sweaty feet isovaleric acidaemia.

II-6.explain: Testing after 48-72 h lets feeding build up metabolites; a positive screen still needs confirmation.
II-6.hook: Heel prick on day 2-3; screen positive = recall, not diagnosis.

checks.q: When is the newborn heel-prick blood spot taken?
checks.why: 48-72 hours, after feeding has started so metabolites accumulate.

checks.q: What follows a positive newborn screening result?
options: Repeat screening at 6 weeks of age
checks.why: A positive screen is not a diagnosis; recall urgently for confirmatory testing.

checks.q: Why check vision at every well-child visit?
checks.why: Amblyopia must be caught early while the visual cortex is plastic.

II-6.explain: Treatment removes the substrate or the trigger; vitamin K and hep B prophylaxis cover universal risks.
II-6.hook: Remove the fuel: phe, lactose, fasting.

checks.q: What is the treatment for galactosaemia?
checks.why: Galactosaemia: remove lactose/galactose; low-phe is for PKU, avoid fasting for MCAD.

checks.q: What daily vitamin D dose is given to newborns?
checks.why: Vitamin D 400 IU daily; all newborns also get vitamin K.

checks.q: Within what time do babies of HBsAg+ mothers need HBIG + vaccine?
checks.why: Within 12 hours of birth to prevent vertical hepatitis B transmission.

II-7.explain: SIDS is what remains when autopsy, death scene and history explain nothing.

checks.q: What upper age limit defines SIDS?
checks.why: SIDS is sudden unexplained death under 1 year, a diagnosis of exclusion.

II-7.explain: Most risk factors impair arousal or oxygenation during sleep: smoke, prone position, soft bedding, heat.

checks.q: Which sleeping arrangement is highest risk for SIDS?
options: Supine on a firm cot mattress
checks.why: Bed-sharing, especially on a sofa or after alcohol, greatly raises SIDS risk.

checks.q: Low birth weight is defined as below what?
checks.why: Low birth weight is <2500 g (5.5 lb), a SIDS risk factor.

II-7.explain: Death needs three things to coincide: a vulnerable baby, a vulnerable age, and a stressor like prone sleep.
II-7.hook: Triple risk: wrong baby, wrong age, wrong night.

checks.q: Which model explains SIDS?
checks.why: Triple-risk: vulnerable infant + critical period + external stressor. Two-hit is Knudson.

checks.q: How does prone sleeping lead to death?
checks.why: Prone sleep causes CO2 rebreathing and hypoxia; the vulnerable infant fails to arouse.

II-7.explain: Peak at 2-4 months when arousal control is immature and maternal protection waning.

checks.q: At what age does SIDS peak?
checks.why: SIDS peaks at 2-4 months, during sleep.

checks.q: Which season shows more SIDS cases?
checks.why: More in winter (overwrapping, infections), boys, preterm and LBW infants.

II-7.explain: Before calling it SIDS you must exclude infection, metabolic disease such as MCAD, and abuse.

checks.q: Which imaging is part of the sudden infant death workup?
checks.why: Full autopsy plus skeletal survey and metabolic screen to exclude abuse and MCAD.

checks.q: What share of deaths over age 1 in Hungary are accidents?
checks.why: Accidents cause 36-40% of deaths after 1 year, the main cause (official answer key).

II-7.explain: Prevention targets each modifiable risk: position, smoke, bedding, sharing; accidents are prevented by barriers.
II-7.hook: Back to sleep, own cot, smoke-free.

checks.q: Which sleep position is recommended for infants?
checks.why: 'Back to sleep' (supine) cut SIDS rates dramatically; side is unstable.

checks.q: Where should the infant sleep?
checks.why: Room-share in own cot on a firm mattress; avoid bed sharing.

checks.q: Which measure prevents childhood drowning?
checks.why: Pool fencing is a proven passive accident-prevention barrier.

II-8.explain: Most infection signs come from the body's reaction (cytokines), not the bug itself.
II-8.hook: Fever, fast heart, fast breath, cold peripheries = host response.

checks.q: Infection signs mainly reflect what?
checks.why: Fever, tachycardia, tachypnoea, poor perfusion are host responses.

II-8.explain: Young infants mount poor localising signs, so any fever is treated as potentially serious.

checks.q: Fever threshold making an infant under 3 months high risk?
checks.why: Any infant <3 months with ≥38 °C is NICE red (high risk).

II-8.explain: Cytokines raise the hypothalamic thermostat via PGE2; vasoconstriction then cools the skin and signals shock.

checks.q: Which mediator raises the hypothalamic set-point in fever?
checks.why: IL-1, IL-6, TNF induce PGE2 in the hypothalamus.

checks.q: Prolonged capillary refill in sepsis is due to what?
checks.why: Peripheral vasoconstriction causes mottling and prolonged CRT: early (compensated) shock.

II-8.explain: Respiratory distress, meningism and petechiae are red flags; tachycardia beyond fever means compensating shock.
II-8.hook: HR too high for the temperature = shock until proven otherwise.

checks.q: Which respiratory rate is a red flag in an infant?
checks.why: RR >60 with grunting is a red flag of serious illness.

checks.q: Tachycardia out of proportion to fever suggests what?
checks.why: Disproportionate tachycardia is an early sign of shock.

II-8.explain: CRP lags a day or two, so an early normal CRP can mislead; procalcitonin rises within hours.
II-8.hook: PCT is quick (hours); CRP is slow (36-48 h).

checks.q: When does CRP peak after onset of bacterial infection?
checks.why: CRP peaks at 36-48 h, so early CRP may falsely reassure; PCT rises in 2-4 h.

checks.q: Normal CSF white cell count is below what?
checks.why: Normal CSF WBC <5/µL; bacterial meningitis also lowers glucose.

II-8.explain: Cultures must precede antibiotics, and their yield depends on blood volume and number of sets.
II-8.hook: Culture first, volume counts, antibiotics within the hour.

checks.q: What most decides blood culture sensitivity?
options: Time of day the sample is drawn
Number of cultures and blood volume
checks.why: Number of cultures and volume of blood decide sensitivity (official answer key).

checks.q: What does a febrile infant under 3 months need?
checks.why: Infant <3 months ≥38 °C: full septic screen (blood, urine, CSF).

checks.q: In a shocked child, when should antibiotics be given?
checks.why: Cultures then antibiotics within 1 hour; never delay for LP.

II-9.explain: Antibiotic choice follows the likely bug, site penetration and local resistance; reviewing early lets you narrow.
II-9.hook: Bug, Body site, Badness, Bias (resistance). Review at 48-72 h.

checks.q: What must be done before starting antibiotics?
checks.why: Culture first: once antibiotics start, culture yield falls.

checks.q: When should antibiotic therapy be reviewed?
checks.why: Review at 48-72 h when cultures return: narrow or stop.

II-9.explain: Bugs change with age; Listeria's cephalosporin resistance is why neonates need amoxicillin/ampicillin.
II-9.hook: Neonate bugs GEL: GBS, E. coli, Listeria.

checks.q: Which organism is typical in neonatal sepsis?
checks.why: Neonatal: GBS, E. coli, Listeria. Older children: pneumococcus, meningococcus, Hib.

checks.q: Why add amoxicillin for neonatal sepsis?
checks.why: Listeria is resistant to cephalosporins, so amoxicillin/ampicillin is needed.

II-9.explain: β-lactams block cell-wall cross-linking; aminoglycosides kill by peak level, β-lactams by time above MIC.

checks.q: What do β-lactams inhibit?
checks.why: β-lactams inhibit PBP transpeptidases; β-lactamase destroys the ring.

checks.q: Aminoglycosides show which type of killing?
checks.why: Aminoglycosides are concentration-dependent (high peaks); β-lactams time-dependent.

II-9.explain: Many drugs harm children through immature metabolism (chloramphenicol) or growing tissues (teeth, cartilage).
II-9.hook: Gray baby, grey teeth, gristle damage.

checks.q: Chloramphenicol in neonates causes what?
checks.why: Immature glucuronidation causes gray baby syndrome; red man is vancomycin.

checks.q: Why avoid ceftriaxone in neonates?
checks.why: Ceftriaxone displaces bilirubin and precipitates with calcium; use cefotaxime.

checks.q: Which drug class risks tendon rupture?
checks.why: Fluoroquinolones: tendon rupture, cartilage damage; aminoglycosides: ATN, ototoxicity.

II-9.explain: Start with culture, then step down: narrow spectrum, oral route, shortest course.

checks.q: When is blood culture taken relative to antibiotics?
checks.why: Blood culture before the first dose, then review at 48-72 h.

checks.q: When can IV antibiotics usually switch to oral?
checks.why: Switch IV to oral once afebrile and improving; use the shortest effective course.

II-9.explain: Empirical regimens match age-specific bugs; viral illnesses need no antibiotics.

checks.q: Empirical treatment for neonatal sepsis?
checks.why: Ampicillin + gentamicin; add/swap cefotaxime if meningitis suspected.

checks.q: First-line for paediatric community-acquired pneumonia?
checks.why: Oral amoxicillin covers pneumococcus, the main CAP pathogen.

checks.q: Which condition needs antibiotics?
checks.why: No antibiotics for colds, bronchiolitis or viral wheeze.

II-10.explain: Lyme is a tick-borne spirochaete infection; mumps is a paramyxovirus targeting glands.

checks.q: Which tick transmits Lyme disease in Europe?
checks.why: Ixodes ricinus in Europe carries Borrelia burgdorferi.

II-10.explain: Borrelia needs a long blood meal to transmit, so early tick removal prevents infection.
II-10.hook: Tick on >24-36 h = risk; mumps incubates 16-18 days.

checks.q: What is the incubation period of mumps?
checks.why: Mumps incubation is 16-18 days; Lyme needs >24-36 h tick attachment.

II-10.explain: Spirochaetes migrate outward from the bite, giving a ring; mumps viraemia seeds glands and CNS.
II-10.hook: Bullseye spreads out; mumps seeds everywhere.

checks.q: Why does erythema migrans clear centrally?
options: Vasculitis of the central dermal vessels
checks.why: Spirochaetes spread outward, leaving central clearing.

checks.q: Why does mumps cause orchitis and meningitis?
checks.why: Viraemia seeds glands and CNS, explaining every complication.

II-10.explain: Lyme stage 2 hits nerves and heart; stage 3 joints and brain. Mumps targets salivary glands, gonads, pancreas, CNS.
II-10.hook: Lyme 2: 'face, brain, heart'. Mumps: post-pubertal orchitis.

checks.q: Which cardiac finding occurs in Lyme stage 2?
checks.why: Early disseminated Lyme: facial palsy, meningitis, carditis with AV block.

checks.q: Mumps orchitis mainly affects which group?
checks.why: Orchitis is typical in post-pubertal males.

II-10.explain: Erythema migrans is diagnosed on sight because serology is often still negative early.
II-10.hook: EM >5 cm + tick bite = treat; no blood test.

checks.q: How is erythema migrans diagnosed?
checks.why: Clinical diagnosis: tick bite and growing erythema >5 cm (official answer key).

checks.q: Which lab finding supports mumps?
checks.why: Mumps raises amylase (salivary); confirm with RT-PCR/IgM.

II-10.explain: Doxycycline is preferred when age allows; CNS or severe heart disease needs IV ceftriaxone.
II-10.hook: Small child: amox; big child: doxy; brain/heart block: ceftriaxone.

checks.q: Erythema migrans in a young child: first choice?
checks.why: Young child amoxicillin; older doxycycline (US any age, 10 days).

checks.q: Lyme with high-grade AV block: treatment?
checks.why: Neuro-Lyme or high-grade block needs IV ceftriaxone.

checks.q: How is mumps prevented?
checks.why: MMR two doses; treatment of mumps is supportive.

II-11.explain: EBV infects B cells; the classic tetrad is fever, sore throat, nodes and big spleen.
II-11.hook: Mono tetrad: Fever, Fauces, Fat nodes, Fat spleen.

checks.q: Infectious mononucleosis is caused by which herpesvirus?
checks.why: EBV = HHV-4; CMV causes a heterophile-negative mono-like illness.

II-11.explain: Saliva spreads it; teens get the full picture while young children are mostly asymptomatic. EBV is oncogenic.
II-11.hook: Kissing teens; Burkitt in Africa, NPC in Asia.

checks.q: Which age group typically gets symptomatic mononucleosis?
checks.why: Most common in teenagers; young children are mild or silent.

checks.q: Which malignancy is linked to EBV?
checks.why: EBV: Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma; Kaposi is HHV-8.

II-11.explain: EBV enters B cells via CD21; CD8 T cells react (atypical cells) and B cells make heterophile antibodies.

checks.q: Which receptor does EBV use to enter B cells?
checks.why: EBV binds CD21 (complement receptor 2) on B cells.

checks.q: Atypical (Downey) lymphocytes are which cells?
checks.why: Downey type II cells are reactive CD8 T cells, not the infected B cells.

checks.q: What produces heterophile antibodies in EBV?
checks.why: Polyclonal B activation yields heterophile antibodies (Monospot).

II-11.explain: Posterior cervical nodes, exudative tonsillitis and hepatosplenomegaly distinguish EBV from strep throat.

checks.q: Which lymph node group is typical of EBV mononucleosis?
checks.why: Posterior cervical lymphadenopathy is classic for EBV.

checks.q: Which blood finding is typical in mononucleosis?
checks.why: Lymphocytosis with raised LFTs (hepatitis).

checks.q: Amoxicillin rash in EBV indicates what?
checks.why: The maculopapular rash is not true allergy; avoid labelling the child.

II-11.explain: Monospot misses many young children, so use VCA IgM; abnormal counts must prompt a leukaemia check.
II-11.hook: Under 5: Monospot lies, VCA IgM tells.

checks.q: Under 4-5 years, which test confirms EBV?
checks.why: Monospot is often negative under 4-5 years; VCA IgM indicates acute infection.

checks.q: Cytopenias or blasts in suspected mono should prompt what?
checks.why: Cytopenias or blasts: exclude leukaemia before calling it EBV.

II-11.explain: Care is supportive; steroids only for complications; the spleen is soft and enlarged, so avoid contact sport.
II-11.hook: No contact sport for 3-4 weeks: protect the spleen.

checks.q: Which drug is useful for uncomplicated mononucleosis?
checks.why: Supportive: rest, fluids, paracetamol; aciclovir is useless.

checks.q: When are steroids indicated in EBV?
checks.why: Steroids only for airway obstruction, haemolysis or thrombocytopenia.

checks.q: How long to avoid contact sport after mononucleosis?
checks.why: 3-4 weeks because of splenic rupture risk.

II-12.explain: Two viruses and one toxin-mediated bacterial rash; the cause dictates treatment.
II-12.hook: Measles Paramyxo, Rubella Toga, Scarlet Strep.

checks.q: Rubella belongs to which virus family?
checks.why: Rubella is a togavirus; measles is a paramyxovirus.

II-12.explain: Measles spreads by aerosol with huge R0; rubella's danger is the fetus in early pregnancy.

checks.q: What is the R0 of measles?
checks.why: Measles R0 12-18, the most contagious infection, aerosol-spread.

II-12.explain: Measles wipes immune memory; rubella crosses the placenta. GAS toxins act as superantigens dilating capillaries.
II-12.hook: Measles erases memory; rubella disrupts organogenesis.

checks.q: What is 'immune amnesia' in measles?
checks.why: Measles kills memory lymphocytes, causing immune amnesia.

checks.q: Scarlet fever rash is caused by what?
checks.why: GAS pyrogenic exotoxins are superantigens causing capillary dilation.

II-12.explain: Measles: prodrome then Koplik spots then rash from head down. Rubella: posterior nodes. Scarlet: sandpaper rash.

checks.q: On which day does the measles rash appear?
checks.why: Rash on day 3-4 after 3 Cs and Koplik spots, spreading from ears downward.

checks.q: Which disease causes foetal injury in 80% of early cases?
checks.why: Rubella: congenital rubella syndrome in 80% (official answer key).

checks.q: Which tongue finding occurs in scarlet fever?
checks.why: Scarlet: strawberry tongue, sandpaper rash, circumoral pallor.

II-12.explain: Measles deaths come mostly from pneumonia; rapid strep tests miss cases so culture confirms.
II-12.hook: Measles kills via lungs; SSPE haunts years later.

checks.q: Commonest cause of death in measles?
checks.why: Measles pneumonia is the commonest cause of death; SSPE comes years later.

checks.q: Which test confirms scarlet fever?
checks.why: Rapid Strep has low sensitivity; throat culture confirms.

II-12.explain: Vitamin A reduces measles mortality; penicillin for scarlet fever prevents rheumatic fever.
II-12.hook: Measles: vitamin A. Scarlet: penicillin 10 days.

checks.q: Which vitamin is given in measles?
checks.why: Vitamin A reduces measles severity and mortality.

checks.q: Why treat scarlet fever with penicillin for 10 days?
checks.why: 10 days phenoxymethylpenicillin prevents rheumatic fever.

checks.q: When is MMR contraindicated?
checks.why: MMR is live: avoid in pregnancy and immunocompromise.

II-13.explain: Helminths are multicellular worms; protozoa are single-celled parasites.

checks.q: Giardia is what kind of parasite?
checks.why: Giardia is a single-celled protozoan; helminths are worms.

II-13.explain: Enterobius is the commonest worm in Europe; Giardia spreads faecal-orally in daycare and streams.
II-13.hook: Puppies give Toxocara; streams give Giardia.

checks.q: Commonest intestinal worm in European children?
checks.why: Enterobius (threadworm/pinworm) is commonest in Europe.

checks.q: Which parasite is classically caught from camping streams?
checks.why: Giardia: faecal-oral, daycare and camping streams.

II-13.explain: Tissue-migrating worms drive a Th2/IL-5 eosinophilia; Giardia flattens villi while Entamoeba invades.

checks.q: Which cytokine drives eosinophilia in worm infections?
checks.why: Th2 cells release IL-5, driving eosinophilia.

checks.q: How does Giardia cause malabsorption?
checks.why: Giardia flattens villi causing fat/lactose malabsorption; Entamoeba invades colon.

II-13.explain: Each parasite has a calling card: perianal itch, leukocoria, greasy stools, bloody diarrhoea, chorioretinitis.

checks.q: Toxocara eye disease can mimic what?
checks.why: Ocular larva migrans causes leukocoria, mimicking retinoblastoma.

checks.q: Which stool type is typical of giardiasis?
checks.why: Giardia: bloating with foul-smelling fatty floating stools.

checks.q: Which liver lobe does amoebic abscess favour?
checks.why: Entamoeba: bloody diarrhoea and right lobe liver abscess.

checks.q: Which brain finding suggests congenital toxoplasmosis?
checks.why: Toxo: diffuse calcifications, chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus; CMV is periventricular.

II-13.explain: Simple bedside tests find most parasites; travel fever must be malaria until films are negative.
II-13.hook: Fever after travel = malaria films now.

checks.q: How is threadworm diagnosed?
checks.why: Sticky tape on the perianal skin picks up eggs.

checks.q: Which finding identifies Entamoeba histolytica?
checks.why: Trophozoites containing RBCs; flask-shaped ulcers on biopsy.

checks.q: Fever after travel to an endemic area: urgent test?
checks.why: Malaria until proven otherwise: urgent thick/thin films.

II-13.explain: Threadworm eggs survive and reinfect, so repeat the dose and treat the household.

checks.q: When is the second mebendazole dose for threadworm?
checks.why: Repeat after 2 weeks to kill newly hatched worms; treat the household.

checks.q: Treatment for giardiasis?
checks.why: Metronidazole (or tinidazole) for Giardia/Entamoeba; albendazole for Toxocara.

checks.q: How long is congenital toxoplasmosis treated?
checks.why: Pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + folinic acid for 12 months.

II-14.explain: Three common viruses: HSV (latent vesicles), parvovirus B19 (red cell precursors), Coxsackie (enterovirus).

checks.q: Parvovirus B19 has which genome?
checks.why: B19 is a parvovirus: small, non-enveloped, single-stranded DNA; causes fifth disease.

II-14.explain: HSV needs direct contact; neonates catch it in the birth canal. Enteroviruses peak in warm months.

checks.q: How do neonates usually acquire HSV?
checks.why: Neonatal HSV comes from maternal genital tract lesions at delivery.

checks.q: When do enterovirus infections peak?
checks.why: Enteroviruses spread faecal-oral, mainly summer/autumn.

II-14.explain: HSV hides in sensory ganglia and reactivates; B19 kills red cell precursors, dangerous when RBC lifespan is short.

checks.q: Where does HSV-1 stay latent?
checks.why: HSV-1 is latent in the trigeminal ganglion; HSV-2 in sacral ganglia.

checks.q: Which receptor does parvovirus B19 use?
checks.why: B19 binds P antigen on erythroid progenitors; CD21 is EBV.

II-14.explain: HSV: cold sores, corneal dendrites, eczema herpeticum. B19: slapped cheek, hydrops. Coxsackie A: HFMD; B: heart.
II-14.hook: Coxsackie A = hAnd foot mouth; B = Bornholm/heart.

checks.q: What is eczema herpeticum?
checks.why: HSV on eczematous skin: punched-out erosions and fever.

checks.q: Which fetal complication does parvovirus B19 cause?
checks.why: B19 causes fetal anaemia leading to hydrops fetalis.

checks.q: Coxsackie B classically causes which condition?
checks.why: Coxsackie B: myocarditis, Bornholm disease; A: HFMD.

II-14.explain: HSV encephalitis targets the temporal lobes; B19 aplastic crisis shows absent reticulocytes.

checks.q: Which test confirms HSV encephalitis?
checks.why: CSF HSV PCR plus MRI showing temporal lobe involvement.

checks.q: Which finding defines an aplastic crisis?
checks.why: Falling Hb with reticulocytopenia.

checks.q: Pregnant woman exposed to B19, IgG positive and IgM negative: management?
checks.why: IgG positive, IgM negative means past infection and immunity: reassure. Weekly ultrasound is for acute infection >20 weeks.

II-14.explain: Never wait for confirmation in suspected HSV encephalitis; aciclovir saves brain tissue.

checks.q: Suspected HSV encephalitis: when to start aciclovir?
checks.why: Start IV aciclovir immediately on suspicion.

checks.q: Duration of IV aciclovir for neonatal HSV?
checks.why: High-dose IV aciclovir 14-21 days.

checks.q: Treatment of fetal anaemia from B19?
checks.why: Fetal anaemia: intrauterine red cell transfusion.

II-15.explain: VZV first causes chickenpox, then hides and can return as dermatomal shingles.

checks.q: What is reactivation of varicella called?
checks.why: Herpes zoster = VZV reactivation (official answer key).

II-15.explain: Contagious from before the rash until all lesions crust, so exclusion lasts until crusting.
II-15.hook: Infectious until every spot is crusted.

checks.q: Until when is a child with chickenpox infectious?
checks.why: Infectious 1-2 days before rash until all lesions have crusted.

II-15.explain: Waves of viraemia produce successive crops; latent virus in sensory ganglia reactivates as T-cell immunity falls.
II-15.hook: Crops = pox in every stage at once.

checks.q: Why are varicella lesions in different stages?
checks.why: Repeated viraemia waves produce crops at different stages.

checks.q: Where does VZV become latent?
checks.why: VZV is latent in dorsal root (sensory) ganglia.

II-15.explain: Chickenpox starts centrally; zoster follows one dermatome. A second fever spike signals bacterial superinfection.
II-15.hook: Fever back after day 3-4 = think GAS.

checks.q: Where does the varicella rash begin?
checks.why: Centripetal rash starting on the trunk.

checks.q: Recurrent fever after day 3-4 of chickenpox suggests what?
checks.why: Returning fever suggests invasive GAS superinfection.

II-15.explain: Varicella is clinical. Maternal timing matters: early pregnancy harms organs, near delivery gives severe neonatal disease.
II-15.hook: -5 to +2 days around birth = danger window.

checks.q: Maternal varicella before which week risks congenital syndrome?
checks.why: Before 20 weeks: congenital varicella syndrome.

checks.q: Maternal rash in which window risks severe neonatal varicella?
checks.why: Rash -5 to +2 days around delivery: no maternal antibodies passed yet.

II-15.explain: Symptom care for healthy children; aciclovir for high-risk; never aspirin (Reye), avoid ibuprofen (GAS skin infection).

checks.q: Which antipyretic is preferred in chickenpox?
checks.why: Paracetamol; ibuprofen linked to invasive GAS, aspirin to Reye syndrome.

checks.q: What is given to high-risk varicella contacts?
checks.why: VZIG for high-risk contacts; aciclovir for neonates/immunocompromised.

checks.q: Varicella vaccine schedule (per notes)?
checks.why: Live attenuated vaccine: 2 doses at 1 and 4 years.

II-16.explain: How deep the infection sits (epidermis, dermis, fascia) determines the clinical picture.
II-16.hook: Depth decides: impetigo top, erysipelas upper dermis, fasciitis deep.

checks.q: What mainly determines the picture of a skin infection?
checks.why: Depth decides the picture: epidermis, dermis or fascia.

II-16.explain: S. aureus and GAS enter through broken skin; tinea capitis is common in young Black children.

checks.q: Which children commonly get tinea capitis (per notes)?
options: Adolescent girls who play contact sport
checks.why: Tinea capitis is common in young African American children.

II-16.explain: Exfoliative toxin splits desmoglein-1 high in the epidermis; necrotising fasciitis kills deep tissue first.
II-16.hook: Desmoglein-1 = SSSS; deep death, mild skin = fasciitis.

checks.q: Which protein does staphylococcal exfoliative toxin cleave?
checks.why: Desmoglein-1 in the granular layer, causing bullous impetigo and SSSS.

checks.q: Why is the skin mild early in necrotising fasciitis?
checks.why: Thrombosed perforators kill deep tissue while skin looks deceptively mild.

II-16.explain: Impetigo crusts are golden; SSSS spares mucosa because desmoglein-3 is intact; fasciitis pain is out of proportion.
II-16.hook: Pain out of proportion = fasciitis until proven otherwise.

checks.q: What crust colour characterises impetigo?
checks.why: Honey-coloured golden crusts; child usually well.

checks.q: What distinguishes SSSS from TEN?
checks.why: SSSS spares mucous membranes (desmoglein-3 intact); TEN involves them.

checks.q: Key early sign of necrotising fasciitis?
checks.why: Pain out of proportion, bullae, crepitus, shock.

II-16.explain: Eye signs mean the orbit is involved and need CT; SSSS blisters are toxin-made and sterile.
II-16.hook: Proptosis or painful eye movement = CT orbit.

checks.q: Proptosis with painful eye movement: which imaging?
checks.why: Orbital cellulitis: CT to look for abscess.

checks.q: In SSSS, where should cultures be taken?
checks.why: Blister fluid is sterile (toxin-mediated); culture the focus.

II-16.explain: Localised impetigo: topical; widespread or bullous: oral anti-staph. Deep or orbital infections need admission.

checks.q: Topical treatment for localised impetigo?
checks.why: Mupirocin topically; oral flucloxacillin if widespread or bullous.

checks.q: Tinea capitis treatment?
checks.why: Tinea capitis needs oral antifungal; topicals don't reach the follicle.

checks.q: Which antibiotic is added in necrotising fasciitis?
checks.why: Urgent surgery + clindamycin (toxin suppression), consider IVIG.

II-17.explain: S. aureus causes pus-forming invasive disease; TSS is a toxin-driven cytokine storm.

checks.q: What mechanism underlies toxic shock syndrome?
checks.why: TSS is a superantigen-induced cytokine storm.

II-17.explain: A third of people carry S. aureus in the nose; TSS links to foreign bodies and packing.
II-17.hook: Tampons, packing, burns: hidden toxin factories.

checks.q: Roughly what proportion carry S. aureus in the nose?
checks.why: Nasal carriage is about one third.

checks.q: Most common cause of osteomyelitis?
checks.why: S. aureus is the most common cause of osteomyelitis.

II-17.explain: Coagulase walls off infection into abscesses; superantigens bypass antigen processing to activate many T cells.

checks.q: What does coagulase do in S. aureus infection?
checks.why: Coagulase builds a fibrin wall leading to abscesses, furuncles, carbuncles.

checks.q: Up to what % of T cells can TSST-1 activate?
checks.why: Superantigens bind MHC II and TCR Vβ, activating up to 20% of T cells.

checks.q: How does MRSA resist methicillin?
checks.why: MRSA has altered PBPs (PBP2a); β-lactamase alone doesn't explain methicillin resistance.

II-17.explain: TSS looks like severe sepsis with a red rash; peeling of palms and soles follows later.
II-17.hook: TSS: fever, red, low BP, then peel.

checks.q: Which skin sign defines acute TSS?
checks.why: High fever, diffuse erythroderma, hypotension, multi-organ failure.

checks.q: When does palm/sole desquamation occur after TSS?
checks.why: Desquamation 1-2 weeks later.

checks.q: How soon after eating does staph food poisoning start?
checks.why: Preformed enterotoxin causes vomiting within 1-6 hours.

II-17.explain: S. aureus bacteraemia seeds bones, joints and valves; staph TSS is toxin-driven so cultures are often sterile.
II-17.hook: Staph TSS cultures negative; strep TSS positive.

checks.q: S. aureus bacteraemia should prompt what?
checks.why: Look for bone, joint, heart focus and repeat cultures.

checks.q: Blood culture in staphylococcal TSS is usually what?
checks.why: Staph TSS usually culture-negative; streptococcal TSS positive.

II-17.explain: Clindamycin stops toxin production; MRSA needs agents that ignore altered PBPs.

checks.q: Why add clindamycin in TSS?
checks.why: Clindamycin inhibits protein synthesis, suppressing toxin production.

checks.q: Which is a first-line drug for MSSA?
checks.why: MSSA: anti-staph penicillins or cefazolin are first-line; vancomycin is reserved for MRSA.

checks.q: Which β-lactam binds MRSA's altered PBPs?
checks.why: Ceftaroline binds altered PBPs; others fail against MRSA.

II-18.explain: Both are clostridial toxin diseases with opposite paralysis: tetanus spastic, botulism flaccid.

checks.q: Which paralysis does botulism cause?
checks.why: C. botulinum causes flaccid paralysis; tetanus spastic.

II-18.explain: Tetanus spores enter deep dirty wounds or unclean cords; infant botulism comes from swallowed spores.

checks.q: Neonatal tetanus is linked to what?
checks.why: Unclean cord care with a poorly immunised mother.

checks.q: Which food is linked to infant botulism?
checks.why: Honey (or juice/dust) spores germinate in the immature gut.

II-18.explain: Tetanospasmin blocks inhibitory transmitters, so muscles contract unopposed; botulinum blocks ACh release.
II-18.hook: Tetanus blocks the brakes; botulinum cuts the accelerator.

checks.q: Tetanospasmin blocks release of which transmitters?
checks.why: It blocks inhibitory GABA/glycine release, causing spasms.

checks.q: What does botulinum toxin cleave?
checks.why: Cleaves SNARE proteins, so no acetylcholine release.

II-18.explain: Tetanus starts at the jaw with the patient fully conscious; botulism starts with cranial nerves and constipation.

checks.q: First sign of tetanus?
checks.why: Jaw first: trismus (lock jaw), then risus sardonicus, spasms.

checks.q: How does botulism paralysis progress?
checks.why: Descending symmetric flaccid paralysis; Guillain-Barré ascends.

II-18.explain: No lab test confirms tetanus; diagnosis rests on spasms with preserved consciousness and sensation.

checks.q: How is tetanus diagnosed?
checks.why: Clinical assessment only; consciousness and sensation preserved.

II-18.explain: Neutralise toxin, remove source, control spasms; tetanus gives no immunity, so vaccinate after recovery.

checks.q: Which antibiotic is used in tetanus?
checks.why: HTIG, debridement, metronidazole, benzodiazepines, ICU.

checks.q: Why vaccinate after recovery from tetanus?
checks.why: Tiny toxin doses don't induce immunity.

checks.q: Which drug class is avoided in infant botulism?
checks.why: Aminoglycosides worsen neuromuscular blockade.

II-19.explain: Osteomyelitis infects bone, septic arthritis the joint; pus in a joint destroys cartilage fast.

checks.q: Which is a surgical emergency?
checks.why: Septic arthritis: pus rapidly destroys cartilage.

II-19.explain: S. aureus dominates; age and host factors shift the list (Kingella toddlers, Salmonella sickle cell).

checks.q: Which organism affects children 6 months-4 years?
checks.why: Kingella kingae is typical in 6 months-4 years.

checks.q: Osteomyelitis after nail puncture through a shoe?
checks.why: Pseudomonas after nail puncture; Salmonella in sickle cell.

II-19.explain: Slow sinusoidal flow in the metaphysis lets bacteria settle; in infants vessels cross the physis into the joint.
II-19.hook: Metaphysis: slow flow, bugs stop and grow.

checks.q: Where does haematogenous osteomyelitis start?
checks.why: Metaphysis, due to slow sinusoidal flow (official answer key).

checks.q: Under 18 months, why does osteomyelitis spread to joints?
checks.why: Transphyseal vessels carry infection into the joint.

II-19.explain: Infants show pseudoparalysis; a septic hip sits in the position of greatest capsular volume.
II-19.hook: Septic hip: Flexed, ABducted, External rotation (FABER).

checks.q: How do infants with bone infection often present?
checks.why: Infants show pseudoparalysis rather than localised pain.

checks.q: Position of a septic hip?
checks.why: Flexion, abduction, external rotation maximise capsular volume.

II-19.explain: X-ray lags 10-14 days, so MRI shows early osteomyelitis; aspiration is diagnostic for septic arthritis.

checks.q: How long can X-ray stay normal in osteomyelitis?
checks.why: X-ray changes appear after 10-14 days.

checks.q: Key diagnostic test for septic arthritis?
checks.why: Aspiration for Gram stain, culture, PCR.

checks.q: Best imaging for early osteomyelitis?
checks.why: MRI is best when ESR high and X-ray normal.

II-19.explain: Anti-staph cover first; short IV then oral works; pus must be drained.
II-19.hook: Short IV, long oral: ~3 weeks total.

checks.q: First-line IV drug for MSSA osteomyelitis?
checks.why: MSSA: nafcillin, oxacillin or IV cefazolin; vancomycin/clindamycin for MRSA.

checks.q: Typical total antibiotic duration for osteomyelitis?
checks.why: Short IV (2-4 days) then oral; about 3 weeks total.

checks.q: Surgical treatment of septic arthritis?
checks.why: Joint washout; drain subperiosteal abscess, remove sequestrum.

II-20.explain: The main congenital musculoskeletal disorders: hip dysplasia, clubfoot, brittle bones and short-limb dwarfism.

checks.q: Which is a congenital bone disorder?
checks.why: OI is congenital; Perthes and SCFE are acquired childhood hip disorders.

II-20.explain: DDH risks reduce space or loosen the hip; OI is a collagen gene defect; achondroplasia an FGFR3 mutation.
II-20.hook: DDH 4 Fs: Female, First-born, Family, Feet-first (breech).

checks.q: Which is a DDH risk factor?
checks.why: Breech, female, first-born, family history, oligohydramnios, tight swaddling.

checks.q: Achondroplasia is caused by what?
checks.why: FGFR3 gain-of-function, linked to older fathers; COL1A1 is OI.

II-20.explain: The acetabulum needs the femoral head inside it to mould; OI's bad collagen gives fragile bones; FGFR3 slows growth plates.
II-20.hook: Overactive FGFR3 = brakes on growth plate.

checks.q: Why does the acetabulum stay shallow in DDH?
checks.why: Without the femoral head in place, the acetabulum fails to mould.

checks.q: Blue sclerae in OI result from defective what?
checks.why: Defective type I collagen: fragile bone, blue sclerae.

checks.q: Achondroplasia limbs are short in which pattern?
checks.why: Rhizomelic (proximal) shortening from poor endochondral growth.

II-20.explain: Early DDH: instability tests; late: limited abduction. Clubfoot has four components: CAVE.
II-20.hook: Clubfoot CAVE: Cavus, Adductus, Varus, Equinus.

checks.q: Late sign of DDH?
checks.why: Later: limited abduction and leg-length discrepancy.

checks.q: Which is a component of clubfoot?
checks.why: Rigid cavus, adductus, varus, equinus.

checks.q: Which hand finding occurs in achondroplasia?
checks.why: Macrocephaly, trident hands, foramen magnum stenosis.

II-20.explain: Ortolani puts the hip back in; Barlow pushes it out. Ultrasound works until the femoral head ossifies.
II-20.hook: Ortolani = Out to In; Barlow = Bye-bye out.

checks.q: Which manoeuvre relocates a dislocated hip?
checks.why: Ortolani relocates; Barlow dislocates a located hip.

checks.q: Hip ultrasound is used until about what age?
checks.why: Ultrasound before ~4.5 months; X-ray once the femoral head ossifies.

checks.q: Which screening test detects scoliosis?
checks.why: Adams forward bend test, then X-ray.

II-20.explain: Treat DDH early and gently, escalating; Ponseti fixes most clubfeet; scoliosis treatment depends on Cobb angle.

checks.q: First-line treatment of DDH under 6 months?
checks.why: Pavlik harness under 6 months, then closed, then open reduction.

checks.q: Which drug treats osteogenesis imperfecta?
checks.why: IV bisphosphonates; clubfoot: Ponseti casting, tenotomy, bracing.

checks.q: Scoliosis Cobb angle 30-40°: management?
checks.why: 10-30° monitor; 30-40° brace; >40-50° surgery.
